title: Knapsack-style Queue Economics & Sizing Experiments (WIP)
body:
Purpose and quick summary:
This is a working spreadsheet-style writeup for an alternate way to reason about continuous-batching sizing and concurrency: treat the system as a knapsack/packing problem over discrete token-service slots, then evaluate p95 latency and throughput impact under realistic queueing shapes. Goal: produce a small set of heuristics and a compact parameterized sheet we can hand to SRE/product to pick Dedicated/Demo cluster sizes and autoscaler headroom.

High-level approach (notes):
- Represent GPU capacity as a fixed number of concurrent slot-units per model variant (slot = a bounded unit of GPU occupancy given a request profile).
- Each incoming request consumes: prefix-k tokens (cacheable) + gen tokens (uncached). We translate token counts into slot-time using empirically measured per-token latency curves (small table below).
- Construct a knapsack where items = request classes (by prompt length & response length distribution) with expected arrival rates. Objective = minimize cost (GPU-hours) subject to p95 latency <= SLO.
- Use Monte Carlo sampling over arrival shapes (Poisson, bursty peak mix with heavy tail) to compute queueing latency.
- Output is: recommended concurrency (min slots), batch-window target, and autoscale headroom to meet p95 under specified traffic envelope.

Key assumptions (tweakable in sheet):
- Token-to-ms mapping for each model/precision (example numbers, replace with bench):
  - rp64 (fp16) 8k context: per-token gen latency = 1.8 ms/token at sustained occupancy; prefix tokens cost ~0.2ms/token when cache hit.
  - int8 quant: gen = 2.1 ms/token, prefix = 0.25 ms/token.
  - small-model (7B equiv) gen = 0.7 ms/token.
- Batch window effect: batching increases per-token latency marginally but reduces per-token cost; effective per-request service time = base + (gen_tokens * per_token) / effective_batch_size. We model batching efficiency as diminishing returns curve: eff(batch) = 1 - alpha / (1 + beta * batch). Alpha and beta are fit from microbenchmarks.
- Concurrency semantics: a single GPU can run N in-flight slots concurrently; each slot's runtime stretches based on batch aggregation.
- Cache hit rate (prefix reuse) is parameterized per route.
- SLO target example: p95 <= 220 ms for interactive routes; throughput target: X QPS.

Spreadsheet sections (what to include):
1) Input tab: request classes, arrival rates, token distributions (p10,p50,p90 for gen length), cache-hit rates, model config (model, precision), cost per GPU-hour.
2) Kernel latency tab: measured per-token curves and batch-efficiency fit parameters.
3) Knapsack discretization: map request classes to discrete slot-time items (rounded to 5ms bins).
4) Monte Carlo sim: arrival sampler (mixture of steady Poisson and occasional microbursts), single-server queueing with parallel servers = number of slots. Compute per-sample p95 and mean.
5) Optimizer tab: search over integer number of slots and batch-window target to find lowest cost meeting latency constraint across x% of sims.
6) Output / recommendation: concise capacity table and recommended autoscaler settings.

Important behavioral observations from early runs (do not treat as final):
- Under mixed workloads (short chat UIs + long generation async jobs), treating slots homogeneously is suboptimal. Needs at least two slot-pools: interactive (low tokens, high p95 sensitivity) and batch/background (high tokens, tolerant SLO). Knapsack solves this by prioritizing items with high latency-sensitivity.
- Slightly enlarging batch-window (10ms->30ms) gives big cost wins for long-gen jobs but can increase p95 for the interactive pool unless you isolate pools or give priority preemption.
- Cache hit-rate variance drives the tail strongly. A route with 85% hit vs 95% hit shows ~30% worse p95 at same capacity.
- Quantized kernels (int8) reduce cost per slot but increase variance in service-time—this feeds the tail. Need to include per-request jitter parameter.

Mini worked example (textual spreadsheet extract):
Inputs:
- Route A: 20 rps, gen tokens dist p50=40, p95=120, cache hit 0.7, interactive SLO p95=220ms
- Route B: 2 rps, gen tokens p50=1200, p95=2500, cache hit 0.05, async SLO p95=2s (much looser)
Model perf (fp16): gen = 1.8ms/token, prefix = 0.2 ms/token, batch-eff params alpha=0.6 beta=0.04
Discretization -> slot-time per request (expected):
- Route A expected service = prefix(0.3*40*0.2) + gen(0.7*40*1.8 / eff_batch) ~ compute per chosen batch. For batch=8, eff ~ 1 - 0.6/(1 + 0.32) = 1 - 0.6/1.32 ~ 0.545 -> effective per-token = 1.8/0.545 = 3.3ms/token -> total ~ (prefix + gen) ~ 0.3*8 + 3.3*40 ~ 133ms (rough).
- Route B expected service = prefix negligible + 1.8*1200/eff_batch -> with batch=16, eff~0.64 => per-token ~2.8ms -> ~ 3360ms.
Knapsack idea: pack a set number of route-A items (short jobs) and route-B items into the fixed slot capacity, simulate arrival shapes and compute p95.

Optimization heuristics we found useful (to include as cells/formulas in sheet):
- Prioritize interactive class in knapsack by scaling its utility with 1/(SLO - mean_service) so that items close to SLO get heavier weight.
- Add a jitter buffer factor = 1 + z * sqrt(var(service_time)/mean), where z tuned for p95. This prevents borderline sizing.
- Search space prune: treat batch-window as discrete choices [4,8,16,32,64] and run integer search over slots.
- Use robustness metric: percent of MC runs that meet p95; pick capacity at 90% robustness for production, 75% for demo clusters.

Practical recommendations (draft):
- For mixed interactive+batch routes, run two pools per model: interactive pool sized for p95 at 90% robustness, background pool sized for throughput cost-optimal packing. Route priority: interactive preempts background when p95 breached.
- Standard initial config for new customer workloads: measure p50/p95 length, fit batch-eff params with microbench, then run the knapsack-sheet auto-search and pick the capacity that meets 90% robustness.
- Autoscaler settings: min = capacity_recommended * 0.8, target_util = 0.6 for interactive pools, cooldown = 45s. For background pools use target_util=0.8 and cooldown=120s.

Open items / TODOs for next iteration:
- Add per-request kernel-switch overheads (e.g., switching quantized kernels when model variant changes).
- Add realistic arrival shapes from real prod traces (request-level token histograms). Need export from observability team: CONFLUENCE-RT-queue-econ-v2 notes -> ask Obs: Liam.
- Validate batch-eff curve for latest kernels on A100/H100 across sequence lengths > 1k.
- Formalize the knapsack solver: currently greedy integer heuristic; try ILP formulation with OR-Tools and compare.
- Explore adaptive batch-window: autoscaler plus tiny controller that adjusts batch-window based on measured p95 drift.

Appendix: quick list of cells/formulas to include in sheet (pseudo):
- service_time(route, batch) = prefix_hits*prefix_tokens*prefix_ms + (1 - prefix_hits)*prefix_tokens*prefix_ms + gen_tokens * per_token_ms / eff(batch)
- eff(batch) = 1 - alpha / (1 + beta * batch)
- jitter_buffer = 1 + z * sqrt(var(service_time)/mean(service_time))
- capacity_slots = ceil(total_required_service_ms_per_second / slot_ms_per_second)
- robustness = count(MC_runs where p95 <= SLO) / total_runs

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally lightweight and experimental; the knapsack framing feels promising because it directly encodes heterogeneous request utilities and lets us reason about packing tradeoffs by class. Please review the example numbers (benchmarks are from Oct 2025 microbench snapshot — need to rerun) and the list of TODOs.
